meta.titre: Temperature scales: fixed points, interpolation and the Kelvin scale

sections.contenu_markdown: Doctors in Yaounde record a patient's fever in degrees Celsius, but a physics teacher in Buea writes the same temperature in kelvin on the board. Both are correct, because they are just two scales for the same hotness. At the GCE you are often given a thermometer with no numbers on it, only the length of the thread at two known temperatures, and you must work out the temperature of an unknown liquid and give it in both scales. The method is short and always the same.

items: The lower fixed point is the temperature of pure melting ice and the upper fixed point is the temperature of steam at standard atmospheric pressure.
A thermometer uses the length of a liquid column that changes steadily with temperature.
Ratios and simple proportions can be solved by cross-multiplication.

sections.titre: Fixed points, the fundamental interval, interpolation and the Kelvin scale
sections.contenu_markdown:
**The Celsius scale.** The lower fixed point (pure melting ice) is $0\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ and the upper fixed point (steam at standard atmospheric pressure) is $100\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$. The **fundamental interval** is the difference between the two fixed points: $100\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ on the temperature scale, which corresponds to the length $l_{100}-l_0$ of thread on an un-calibrated thermometer.

**Linear interpolation.** If the thread expands uniformly, the temperature $\theta$ at which the thread has length $l_\theta$ is found by proportion:

$$\theta=\frac{l_\theta-l_0}{l_{100}-l_0}\times 100\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$$

where $l_0$ is the length at the lower fixed point and $l_{100}$ the length at the upper fixed point. The numerator is the distance the thread has risen above the ice mark; the denominator is the fundamental interval in length.

**The Kelvin (absolute) scale.** The kelvin (K) is the SI unit of temperature. **Absolute zero** is the lowest possible temperature, $0\ \mathrm{K}=-273\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$. A change of one kelvin equals a change of one degree Celsius, so the scales differ only by a shift of 273:

$$T(\mathrm{K})=\theta(^\circ\mathrm{C})+273 \qquad\qquad \theta(^\circ\mathrm{C})=T(\mathrm{K})-273$$

| Point | Celsius | Kelvin |
|---|---|---|
| Absolute zero | $-273\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ | $0\ \mathrm{K}$ |
| Melting ice (lower fixed point) | $0\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ | $273\ \mathrm{K}$ |
| Steam (upper fixed point) | $100\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ | $373\ \mathrm{K}$ |

Write kelvin readings as $308\ \mathrm{K}$, never "$308\,^\circ\mathrm{K}$".

variantes.nom: Finding a length from a temperature
variantes.quand_utiliser: When the temperature is given and you must find where the thread will be.
variantes.contenu_markdown: Rearrange the proportion: $l_\theta=l_0+\dfrac{\theta}{100}\times(l_{100}-l_0)$. For example, halfway between the fixed points ($50\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$) the thread is exactly halfway between $l_0$ and $l_{100}$.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When a question gives a rise or fall in temperature and asks for it in the other scale.
variantes.contenu_markdown: A **difference** has the same numerical value in both scales, because the size of one kelvin equals the size of one Celsius degree. A rise from $20\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ to $60\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ is a rise of $40\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, which is also a rise of $40\ \mathrm{K}$. Only a **temperature reading** needs the shift of 273.

sections.enonce_markdown:
An un-calibrated mercury thermometer has a thread of length $4.0\ \mathrm{cm}$ in pure melting ice and $24.0\ \mathrm{cm}$ in steam from water boiling at standard pressure. It is then placed in a cup of warm water and the thread is $11.0\ \mathrm{cm}$ long.

(a) Find the fundamental interval in length.

(b) Find the temperature of the water in $^\circ\mathrm{C}$ and in kelvin.

etapes.action: Identify the lengths at the fixed points.
etapes.justification: The ice point is the lower fixed point and the steam point is the upper fixed point.
It is the difference between the two fixed-point lengths.

etapes.action: Calculate how far the thread has risen above the ice mark.
etapes.justification: Only the rise above $l_0$ counts for the temperature.
The thread expands uniformly, so temperature is proportional to the rise.
Add 273 to a Celsius temperature to get kelvin.

sections.conclusion_markdown: **(a)** Fundamental interval $=20.0\ \mathrm{cm}$. **(b)** The water is at **$35\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$**, which is **$308\ \mathrm{K}$**.

items.pourquoi_faux: The thread does not start at zero length. At $0\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ it already has length $l_0$, which must be subtracted from both the top and the bottom.
The 100 is the size of the fundamental interval, not the shift between the scales. Absolute zero is at $-273\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$.

items.erreur_markdown: “A temperature rise of $30\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ is a rise of $303\ \mathrm{K}$.”
items.pourquoi_faux: The shift of 273 applies to a temperature reading, not to a change in temperature. One kelvin is the same size as one Celsius degree.
items.correction_markdown: A rise of $30\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ is a rise of $30\ \mathrm{K}$.

items.pourquoi_faux: The kelvin is the SI unit itself and is written without the degree sign.

items.enonce_markdown:
Convert the following.

(a) $37\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ to kelvin

(b) $373\ \mathrm{K}$ to degrees Celsius

(c) $250\ \mathrm{K}$ to degrees Celsius

An un-calibrated thermometer shows a thread of $5.0\ \mathrm{cm}$ in melting ice and $25.0\ \mathrm{cm}$ in steam at standard pressure. In a basin of warm water the thread is $14.0\ \mathrm{cm}$ long. Find the temperature of the water in $^\circ\mathrm{C}$ and in $\mathrm{K}$.
items.solution_markdown:
Fundamental interval $=25.0-5.0=20.0\ \mathrm{cm}$.

Rise above the ice mark $=14.0-5.0=9.0\ \mathrm{cm}$.

$\theta=\dfrac{9.0}{20.0}\times100=$ **$45\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$**.

$T=45+273=$ **$318\ \mathrm{K}$**.

items.enonce_markdown:
The thread of a certain thermometer is $2.5\ \mathrm{cm}$ long at the lower fixed point and $17.5\ \mathrm{cm}$ long at the upper fixed point.

(a) How many centimetres does the thread move for each degree Celsius?

(b) Find the temperature when the thread is $8.5\ \mathrm{cm}$ long.

(c) A liquid is at $328\ \mathrm{K}$. How long is the thread in this liquid?
items.solution_markdown:
(a) Fundamental interval $=17.5-2.5=15.0\ \mathrm{cm}$ for $100\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, so the movement is $15.0/100=$ **$0.15\ \mathrm{cm}/^\circ\mathrm{C}$**.

(b) $\theta=\dfrac{8.5-2.5}{15.0}\times100=\dfrac{6.0}{15.0}\times100=$ **$40\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$**.

(c) First convert to Celsius: $\theta=328-273=55\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$. Then $l=2.5+0.15\times55=2.5+8.25=$ **$10.75\ \mathrm{cm}$**.

Check: $\dfrac{10.75-2.5}{15.0}\times100=55\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$.

items_markdown: Fixed points: $0\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ (pure melting ice) and $100\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ (steam at standard pressure); the fundamental interval is the difference between them.
Interpolation: $\theta=\dfrac{l_\theta-l_0}{l_{100}-l_0}\times100$. Always subtract $l_0$ on top and bottom.
Kelvin: $T(\mathrm{K})=\theta(^\circ\mathrm{C})+273$; absolute zero is $0\ \mathrm{K}=-273\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$; write K, not $^\circ\mathrm{K}$.
A temperature change has the same number in kelvin and in degrees Celsius.
Give the final answer with the right unit and, when asked, in both scales.
